WHEN LIFE INTERRUPTS THE MUSIC; Series 2 What Life Teaches Us Outside the Music Sometimes, the lessons that shape us most are learned when we are no longer standing on the stage. For many years, I thought some of my most important lessons would come from music itself. From rehearsals, performances, teaching, leading musicians, studying an instrument, standing in front of an ensemble and trying to bring different people together to create one sound. But over time, I discovered that some of my deepest lessons about leadership, responsibility, relationships, purpose, sacrifice, and letting go came from experiences that had very little to do with playing a note. One of those experiences was particularly difficult. I had to make the decision to dissolve a music band I had built and nurtured for over seven years. It was not simply a band. It was a community. At its peak, I had more than 30 consistent band members—young people brought together by a shared purpose, a vision, and the influence of the work we were doing together. Many of them were people I had personally mentored. I had watched some of them grow musically. I had invested time in them. I had taught them. I had corrected them. I had encouraged them. I had watched relationships develop, talents mature, confidence increase, and people discover abilities they may not have known they possessed. So when the time came to dissolve the band, it was not an easy decision. There was history attached to it. There were memories. There were relationships. There was emotional investment. And there was the uncomfortable question: “How do you let go of something you spent years building?” That experience taught me lessons that music alone could never have taught me. When Building Something Is Not the Same as Keeping It Forever We often celebrate people who build. People who build a business, career, team, ministry, an institution, a family, or a reputation, a community. But we don’t talk enough about another aspect of leadership: Knowing when something has reached the point where it needs to change—or even end. There is a natural tendency to protect what we have invested in. The more time we spend building something, the harder it becomes to imagine letting it go. Seven years is a long time. Thirty people are not simply numbers on a list. They represent conversations, rehearsals, challenges, birthdays, performances, disagreements, laughter, growth, mistakes, achievements, and countless moments that become part of your personal history. So dissolving the band felt, in many ways, like closing a significant chapter of my life. But I eventually learned that the value of something is not always measured by how long it continues. Sometimes, something can have fulfilled an important purpose even if it does not continue indefinitely. The People Were More Important Than the Band One of the things I had to remind myself was that the band was never really about me. It is about people. Young people with potential. People who needed direction. People who needed an environment where they could develop. People who needed someone to believe in them. People who needed opportunities to discover what they could become. That changed the way I viewed the decision. Although the structure was ending, the influence did not have to end. The years of mentorship had already happened. The skills people acquired remained with them. The confidence they developed remained. The relationships remained. The experiences remained. The lessons remained. And that taught me something important about leadership: Sometimes, what you build is temporary, but what you build into people can outlive the structure itself. Almost all the people I had with me then have influenced their various spaces as team leaders, music producers, artists, professinal musicians, ministry leaders, song writers, movie directors, among others. That, for me, became one of the most meaningful lessons from that chapter. The Pain of Letting Go There is a certain kind of pain that comes with ending something you did not necessarily want to lose. It is different from failure. Sometimes, you are not walking away because the thing had no value. You are walking away precisely because you understand that the circumstances surrounding it have changed. That distinction matters. There were memories I did not want to lose. There were people I cared about. There were dreams associated with the band. There were things I imagined we would accomplish together. But leadership sometimes requires making decisions based on what is necessary rather than what is emotionally comfortable. And that is not always easy. I had to accept that loving something does not automatically mean you must keep it in its current form forever. What the Band Taught Me About Leadership Leading a group of young musicians for several years taught me that leadership is not simply about having a vision. It is about people. People have different personalities, different motivations, different levels of commitment, different family circumstances, different aspirations, different rates of growth, different ideas about what they want from the journey. When you bring people together around a common purpose, you discover very quickly that leadership is more complex than simply giving instructions. You have to communicate, listen, correct, encourage, make difficult decisions, manage expectations. And sometimes, you have to accept that not everyone will remain on the journey for the same length of time. That was a valuable lesson for me. Influence Is Bigger Than Position When I look back at those years, one thing stands out to me. The most significant achievement was not necessarily the music we performed. It was the people who were influenced along the way. Some of the young people I mentored came into the group with limited confidence. Some had undeveloped musical abilities. Some simply needed an opportunity. Over time, they grew. And watching that growth reminded me that influence is not always measured by the size of an organisation or the visibility of a platform. Sometimes, influence is simply seeing someone become better because you were willing to invest in them. That is one of the reasons the decision to dissolve the band was difficult. I wasn’t just thinking about an organisation. I was thinking about people. The Lesson of Letting Go One of the hardest lessons leadership teaches us is that not everything we build belongs to us forever. We are custodians for a season. We may start something, develop it, nurture it, strengthen it, give it direction, and eventually, circumstances may require us to release it. That can feel like failure if our definition of success is simply continuation. But perhaps success should sometimes be measured by impact. If something existed for seven years and positively influenced people, developed talents, created relationships, and helped young people grow, its value does not disappear simply because the structure eventually came to an end. The ending does not erase the journey. Life Taught Me That People Are Not Projects This is another lesson I continue to carry. When you are leading people, it can be tempting to think in terms of outcomes. Who is improving? Who is committed? Who is performing well? Who is meeting expectations? Who is contributing? But people are not projects. They have lives beyond the role they occupy in your organisation. They have families, dreams, fears, challenges, responsibilities, personal journeys. Sometimes, leadership requires us to remember that the person matters more than the position they occupy. The band gave me many opportunities to learn this. And those lessons have influenced the way I now think about teaching, mentoring, music education, and leadership. What Remained After the Band Ended? This is perhaps one of the most interesting parts of the story. The band ended but the work did not become meaningless. The musicians had learned. The relationships had happened. The mentorship had happened. The performances had happened. The memories had been created. The experience had shaped me. And many of the people who passed through that chapter had been changed by it in one way or another. This helped me understand something I now consider fundamental: An ending can be real without making everything that came before it meaningless. – Victor Adenola Sometimes, we need to stop measuring a chapter by whether it lasted forever. Instead, ask: What did it produce while it lasted? This Lesson Followed Me Into Other Areas of Life The lessons from that experience did not stay within music. They followed me into family. Into teaching. Into professional relationships. Into leadership. Into business. Into mentoring. Into how I approach new opportunities. I became more conscious of the difference between building something and being defined by something. I became more willing to accept that seasons change. I became more aware that people can be part of your journey without necessarily being part of every chapter. And I became more comfortable with the idea that sometimes, moving forward requires releasing something behind you. The Music May End, But the Lesson Continues Looking back now, I don’t only remember the difficulty of dissolving the band. I remember what those seven years produced. I remember the young people, the music, the mentoring, the growth, the relationships, and the lessons. That experience taught me that leadership is not about holding on to people forever. It is about helping people become better while you have the opportunity to influence them. It taught me that purpose is not always attached to a permanent structure. And it taught me that sometimes, the responsible thing to do is to recognise when a chapter has served its purpose and have the courage to close it. What Life Taught Me From That Experience If I were to summarise the lessons from that chapter, they would be these: What you build may not last forever, but its impact can. Leadership is about people, not just structures. Mentorship can outlive the platform through which it happened. Letting go is sometimes an act of responsibility, not failure. Not every ending needs to be interpreted as a loss. People may leave a chapter without leaving your influence. A successful chapter does not have to become a permanent institution to have been worthwhile. And perhaps the lesson that remains closest to me: “Sometimes, leadership means knowing when to hold on, and sometimes it means having the courage to let go. What matters is what you leave in the people you have influenced.” — Victor Adenola A Reflection for You Perhaps there is something in your life that you are holding on to simply because you have invested so much into it. Ask yourself: Is the value of this thing found only in its continuation, or has it already fulfilled an important purpose? And if the time comes to let it go, remember: Ending a chapter does not erase the story. The people you helped. The lessons you learned. The skills you developed. The lives you touched. The person you became. Those things remain. Sometimes, the most difficult decision you make as a leader is not deciding what to build next, but deciding what you must release so that you can move into the next season. Coming Next — Series 3: Finding Yourself in the Interruption When a familiar chapter ends, something deeper often follows. Who am I now? What happens when the role, platform, career, relationship, routine, or structure that once gave you a sense of identity is no longer there?
